hints: Notice in the diagram that $p$ is horizontal while weight $W$ acts vertically downward, but $q$ is vertical upward.
Recall that work done by or against a constant force is $F$ times displacement in the direction of $F$, so only displacement parallel to $W$ counts.
Use the wording starts and finishes at rest to argue there is no net change in kinetic energy, so net work equals the gain in gravitational potential energy $Wq$.
walkthrough: Identify the force doing work on the weight. Gravity and the supporting force act vertically with magnitude related to $W$, while the motion has a horizontal part $p$ and a vertical rise $q$.
State the rule for work: $work = F \times d \cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement. Only the component of displacement along the force contributes.
Consider the horizontal motion $p$. Here $\theta = 90^\circ$ between vertical weight $W$ and horizontal displacement $p$, so $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and work over $p$ is zero.
Consider the vertical motion $q$. This is parallel and opposite to gravity, so work done on the weight to raise it is $W \times q$. This is stored as increase in gravitational potential energy.
Check kinetic energy. The weight starts and finishes at rest, so change in kinetic energy is zero and no extra net work is needed for speed.
Therefore total work done on the weight is $Wq$. This is option C.

options.A: Horizontal distance $p$ is perpendicular to weight $W$, so the component of displacement in the direction of $W$ is zero and no work is done over $p$.
options.B: Only the vertical height $q$ is parallel to $W$. Adding $p$ and $q$ incorrectly treats perpendicular displacements as if both do work against gravity.
options.C: Work against gravity is $W$ times vertical rise $q$. With zero change in kinetic energy, this equals the gain in gravitational potential energy.
options.D: Distance $r$ is the diagonal from X to Y, but work uses only the component of $r$ along $W$, which is $q$, not the full length $r$.
